n: With thousands pressing in so tightly they trample one another, Jesus first warns His disciples about hypocrisy. Like yeast in dough, a little pretense quietly spreads through everything.

f.g: Yeast or fermented dough; in scripture often a symbol of corrupting influence.
Greek hypokrisis, originally an actor playing a part behind a mask.

n: Pretending won’t work forever. Everything hidden will eventually be exposed, so it is better to be genuine now.

f.w: nothing covered, that shall not be revealed

n: Words whispered privately will one day be shouted from the rooftops. Flat roofs were places where public announcements could be made.

f.g: Inner rooms, private chambers.
Flat roofs used for living space and for making announcements.

n: Calling His disciples “friends,” Jesus tells them not to fear persecutors. The worst they can do is kill the body, which is not the end of a person.
The One to reverently fear is God, who holds eternal destiny in His hands. Holy fear of God drives out fear of people.

f.g: Greek geenna (Gehenna), named for the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a symbol of final judgment.

n: Sparrows were so cheap that you got five for two pennies — one was thrown in free. Yet God remembers each one.

f.g: Small Roman copper coins (assarion), each worth a fraction of a day’s wage.

f.w: not one of them is forgotten before God

n: God knows us down to the number of hairs on our heads. If He cares for sparrows, how much more does He value each of His children?

f.w: the very hairs of your head are all numbered

n: Those who openly acknowledge Christ before others will be acknowledged by Him before God’s angels.
Those who deny Him will be denied. Our loyalty to Christ now shapes how He will stand with us later.
Words spoken against the Son of Man can be forgiven, but willfully rejecting the witness of the Holy Ghost after receiving it cannot. Latter-day revelation explains this unpardonable sin.
When disciples are hauled before religious or civil authorities, they shouldn’t worry in advance about defending themselves.

f.g: Civil officials and judges.
Don’t be anxious.

n: The Holy Ghost will give them the right words at the right moment. This promise is repeated to missionaries in the latter days.

f.w: the Holy Ghost shall teach you in the same hour

n: Someone in the crowd interrupts, asking Jesus to settle a family dispute over inheritance. Rabbis were often asked to rule on such matters.

f.g: Under the law, an elder brother received a double share.

n: Jesus declines to act as an arbiter. His mission is not to divide property but to address the heart.

f.g: One who divides an estate — an arbitrator.

n: He warns against every form of greed. Life isn’t measured by how much we own.

f.g: Greed, the craving for more.

f.w: abundance of the things which he possesseth

n: Jesus tells a parable about a rich man whose land produced a huge harvest. The wealth itself isn’t the problem — it’s what he does with it.

f.g: Produced a bumper crop.

n: He talks only to himself. His problem: too much stuff and not enough room. He never thinks of God or of the hungry.

f.g: Store.

n: His solution is bigger barns. Notice how many times he says “I” and “my” — his world revolves around himself.

f.g: Count the possessives: my fruits, my barns, my goods, my soul.

n: He plans an easy life for years ahead: eat, drink, and enjoy. He assumes he controls his future.
God calls him a fool: his life ends tonight. All his hoarded wealth will go to someone else. He prepared for everything except eternity.

f.g: In Hebrew thought, a fool is one who lives as if there is no God.

f.w: this night thy soul shall be required of thee

n: This is the fate of everyone who hoards for themselves but isn’t rich in the things that matter to God — faith, love, generosity.
Turning to His disciples, Jesus tells them not to be consumed with anxiety over food and clothing.

f.g: Don’t worry anxiously — not a ban on planning.

n: Life is bigger than food, and the body is more than its clothing. God, who gave the greater gifts, will surely provide the lesser.

f.g: Food.
Clothing.

n: Ravens don’t farm or store up food, yet God feeds them. Ravens were unclean birds under the law — if God feeds even them, how much more His children!
Worry can’t add a single moment to your life — or an inch to your height. It accomplishes nothing.

f.g: About 18 inches; here possibly a measure of lifespan rather than height.

n: If worry can’t even do something so small, why let it control the bigger things of life?

f.g: Worry.

n: Wildflowers don’t labor or weave cloth, yet they are dressed more beautifully than King Solomon at his most splendid.

f.g: Probably the wildflowers that blanket Galilean hills in spring.

n: If God clothes the grass, which lasts only a day before being burned as fuel, He will certainly take care of you. Jesus gently chides their small faith.

f.g: Dried grass was used to heat clay ovens.

n: Don’t make food and drink your main pursuit, and don’t be anxious or unsettled about them.

f.g: Anxious, tossed back and forth like a ship.

n: These are the things the whole world chases after. Your Father already knows what you need.

f.g: The Gentiles — those who don’t know God.

n: Make God’s kingdom your priority, and He will provide what you need along the way.

f.w: seek ye the kingdom of God

n: One of the tenderest verses in scripture: do not fear, little flock. It delights the Father to give you His kingdom.

f.g: Joyful will, delight.

n: Turn earthly wealth into heavenly treasure by giving to those in need. Heaven’s “purses” never wear out, and nothing stored there can be stolen or ruined.

f.g: Money purses that don’t wear out.
Gifts to the poor.

n: Our hearts follow our treasure. What we invest in reveals and shapes what we love.
Be dressed and ready with lamps lit. Long robes were tucked into the belt for active work; lamps were kept burning for a night arrival.

f.w: Let your loins be girded about
f.g: Tuck up your robe — be ready for action.

n: Be like servants waiting up for their master to return from a wedding feast, ready to open the door the moment he knocks.

f.g: Wedding feasts could last days, so the return time was uncertain.

n: In an astonishing reversal, the master himself puts on an apron and serves the faithful servants. This is how Christ treats those who wait for Him.
Even if he comes in the middle of the night or close to dawn, the servants found ready will be blessed.

f.g: The Jews divided the night into three watches; the second and third covered roughly 10 p.m. to 6 a.m.

n: A homeowner who knew when a burglar was coming would stay alert and protect his house.

f.g: Master of the household.
Literally “dug through” — houses with mud-brick walls could be broken into by digging.

n: So be ready always, because Christ will return when people least expect it.

f.w: the Son of man cometh at an hour when ye think not

n: Peter asks whether this teaching is for the apostles specifically or for everyone.
Jesus answers with a question about the faithful steward — a trusted servant put in charge of feeding the household on time. Leaders have special responsibility.

f.g: A household manager entrusted with another’s property.
At the proper time.

n: That servant will be blessed when the master returns and finds him faithfully at work.

f.g: Doing his duty.

n: The faithful servant will be given charge of everything the master owns — faithfulness in small things leads to greater trust.

f.w: ruler over all that he hath

n: But if the servant assumes the master won’t be back soon and starts abusing others and partying, he betrays his trust.
The master will arrive unexpectedly and punish him severely, placing him among the unfaithful.

f.g: Cut him in pieces — a vivid image of severe judgment.

n: A servant who knew what his master wanted and deliberately ignored it will receive heavy punishment. Knowledge increases accountability.

f.g: Lashes from a whip.

n: Those who sinned in ignorance receive lighter judgment. The principle: the more we are given, the more is expected of us.

f.w: unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required

n: Jesus came to kindle a fire on the earth — a refining, purifying fire of the gospel and the Spirit. He longs to see it blazing.
Before that, He must pass through a “baptism” of suffering — His Atonement and death. He feels the weight of it pressing on Him until it is finished.

f.w: a baptism to be baptized with

f.g: Distressed, pressed, constrained.

n: Jesus brings ultimate peace, but in the short term His message will divide people — some accepting, others rejecting.
Even within a single household, people will take sides over Him.

f.g: A family of five split by different responses to Christ.

n: These words echo Micah’s prophecy of family conflict. Choosing Christ can strain even the closest relationships.

f.w: The father shall be divided against the son

n: Turning to the crowd, Jesus notes how well they read the weather: clouds from the Mediterranean in the west mean rain.

f.g: The Mediterranean Sea lies west of Israel.

n: A south wind from the desert brings scorching heat. They read these signs perfectly.

f.g: Wind from the Negev and Arabian deserts.

n: They can forecast weather but fail to recognize the most important sign of all — that the Messiah is among them.
Why can’t they judge for themselves what is right? They have enough evidence to decide.

f.g: On your own, without needing a sign.

n: If you are being taken to court, settle with your opponent on the way before the judge hands you over to be imprisoned. Make peace with God now, before judgment comes.

f.g: Drag.
Make every effort.

n: Once in prison, you won’t leave until the last tiny coin is paid. Better to reconcile now while there is time — repentance is urgent.

f.g: Greek lepton, the smallest copper coin.
